route.instructions:
The state is a request to a coding agent. Decide when the strong model's analysis must happen: before the first edit or during the work. Prewalk lets a strong model inspect and plan, then hands the work to a faster, cheaper model; it pays off only when the hard part can be settled before implementation and the remaining work is bounded.

`request` is the task to classify and is authoritative. `previous_request` and `previous_response`, when present, are the user's earlier request and the agent's last reply. Use them only to resolve what a short or referential request points at ("do that", "continue", "fix what you found"). A request that stands on its own is classified on its own words, whatever came before it.

Judge where analysis is needed, not how large or hard the task is. Volume of work never makes a task a prewalk candidate, and neither does difficulty alone. Needing a plan is not enough: the hard part must be settled by the time the first edit is made. A wrong prewalk costs more than a missed one. If torn between prewalk and primary, choose primary. If torn on whether a small task is worth any hand-off, choose direct.

criteria.prewalk: Both hold: starting correctly needs real up-front investigation, repository understanding, diagnosis, design, or planning; and once that fixes the approach, implementation and verification are bounded enough for a faster model. Tracing an unfamiliar subsystem before a localized change; reading several interacting files before implementing a clear design; diagnosing a bug down to a concrete fix whose implementation is straightforward; a migration or refactor whose hard part is finding the right transformation and everything it touches.
criteria.primary: The strong model must stay active during implementation, debugging, or validation, so handing off at the first edit would be premature. Unresolved races, concurrency, or invariant problems; subtle state-machine or lifecycle changes; a cause that may remain unclear after initial inspection; high-risk changes that need iterative implementation and verification; difficult algorithms; work where the first edit is only the start of the hard part.
criteria.direct: No up-front phase worth handing off from: explanations and read-only questions; trivial or mechanical edits; fully specified changes with an obvious implementation; tiny localized fixes; requests that involve no implementation.
